**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No.
   - **Where:** the hero image, roughly x 340–940, y 92–422, about 40% of the content column and the largest thing on the page.
   - **What the viewer sees:** a generic grey person silhouette on a dark brown gradient. It says nothing about Ines Varga, the novel, the island, or an evening at a bookshop. The viewer looks there first and finds nothing, so the page reads as unfinished, or as a broken image. The headline then has to do all the work.
   - **Why:** This is common sense. The catalog's source is off the approved list, so it is argued here on its own terms. The biggest area of the page is spent on an empty slot.
   - **What would make it fine:** if a real author photo failed to load in this capture, this is not a design problem. Check it in a live browser.
   - **Fix:** put in a real picture that gives the headline something it can't say alone. That could be the author, the book cover, or a picture of the island. If no picture is available, shrink or drop the slot so the date and headline lead.
   - **Kind:** defect. **Weight:** major.

Extra point outside the checklist: a reader new to the page can't tell where the event is. The page gives no venue or address, and no year. "Find us" in the nav suggests the shop, but the person deciding to book has to guess. Since this is a date-and-place commitment, that gap is a defect. **Fix:** add one line, such as "At Margin Books, [street]", next to the date. **Weight:** minor to major, depending on whether the shop has more than one branch.

**What's working.**
- **The ask names one exact act:** "Book a free seat". It says what the viewer gets and what it costs, so the viewer has nothing left to work out.
- **The copy is concrete and sounds human:** a reading, a short talk about the island, questions, and wine from 6.30 pm. The viewer can picture the evening before booking.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the silhouette is the intended design or an author photo that failed to load. Check the live page.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (main image and headline make one idea).

sections.report:
Walk (working notes):

First read: the eye goes first to the dark 600×330 picture block (y 92–422). It is the largest and darkest mass on a white page. Next it drops to the bold headline at y 470–550, then the dark button. This is an event page for a small bookshop, aimed at local readers. It feels calm and plain.

What matters first:
- Does one element dominate? Yes. The dark picture dominates by size and value, and the headline clearly leads the text.
- Are the text levels distinct? Yes. I count the date (about 14 px, bold, rust), the headline (about 34 px, bold), the body (about 16 px, regular, grey-dark), the button (about 15 px, bold, reversed), the logo (about 19 px, bold) and the nav (about 14 px, regular, grey). There are no near-collisions in the content column. The date and the body are close in size but differ in weight and colour.
- Do headings differ by more than size? Yes. The headline is bold and darker than the regular body text.

All lines are yes, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
1. **Clear reading order.** The headline at x 340–905, y 470–550 is about twice the size of the body text and bold against regular. The rust date sits above it as a small, bold kicker in a different colour. So the order goes date, then what the event is, then the details, then the button, with no levels fighting for attention. That order only works because size, weight and colour each do a separate job. Keep the rust colour for the date only.
2. **The button closes the column clearly.** "Book a free seat" (x 340–502, y 625–672) is the only filled dark shape below the picture. It is the obvious last stop, even though its label is small.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **The picture may be a placeholder.** It is a grey head-and-shoulders silhouette on a dark gradient, not a photo of Ines Varga. It is also the first thing the eye lands on, so if this is the live design, the most dominant element on the page tells the viewer nothing. Check in a live browser whether a real author photo loads there. If it is meant to stay a placeholder, the hierarchy should be rebalanced so the headline leads. This belongs to the pictures section rather than this one, so it's flagged here and not counted as a finding.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I've finished the walk and the deep read, and I'm writing the report now.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** No.
   - **Where:** the header bar (y 0–59). The "Margin Books" wordmark (x 48–175) looks centred at about y=28, and the nav ("Events" to "Find us", x 952–1232) at about y=31. Their baselines also look a pixel or two apart.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the two sides of the header look like they were meant to line up and just missed. It's a small "not quite finished" note at the very top of an otherwise tidy page.
   - **Why:** a placement that is neither clearly aligned nor clearly off it makes the eye waver (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance").
   - **Fix:** put the wordmark and the nav on one shared baseline, or centre both on the bar's midline. Measure it in the browser before changing anything, because by eye the gap is only 2–3 px.
   - Defect (craft), minor.

**What's working.**
- **One left edge.** The picture, date, headline, description and button all start at exactly x=340 and stay inside one 600 px column. The whole event reads as a single unit, and the eye drops straight from picture → date → headline → description → "Book a free seat" with nothing pulling it sideways.
- **Spacing within the event.** The date sits nearer the headline (about 15 px) than the picture (about 26 px), so it reads as the headline's label, not a caption to the photo. The large empty side bands and the space below the button are gathered into a few big areas, not scattered, which makes this one event feel like the only thing on the page. A centred single column suits a page with one thing to do.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (exact alignment, no near-misses)

I've finished the walk and the deep read, and the Text report follows.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** No. The two-line headline (x 340–904, y ≈ 475–550) breaks "An evening with Ines Varga on her / new novel, The Salt Year". The break falls between "her" and "new novel", which splits the phrase "on her new novel". Line one ends on a word that leads nowhere, so the reader pauses at "her" and then has to join it back to line two. A break at "An evening with Ines Varga / on her new novel, The Salt Year" puts the author on one line and the book on the other. Each line then holds one idea, and the book's title gets a line of its own to land on. The direction of the fix is to set the break by hand with a non-breaking space or a line break that is kept at other widths. This is taste, or common sense: the catalog's source for breaks in headings is unverified. Weight: minor.
2. **Copy that the checklist has no line for: the date may be wrong.** The date line (x 340–538, y ≈ 447–462) says "Thursday 13 November, 7 pm" and gives no year. In 2026, 13 November falls on a Friday; it was a Thursday in 2025. This is the one line a reader will act on. If the event is in 2026, half the readers will turn up on the wrong evening or think it is the wrong date, and the other half will trust the weekday. If the event was in 2025, it is already over and the page is still offering "Book a free seat". The fix is to check the date. Then make the weekday and the date agree, or add the year. If the event is over, show that it is past. This is a defect, as long as the event is meant for 2026 or the page is still live. Weight: major if either is true, otherwise none.
3. **Copy, not a checklist line: the book title is set in roman.** "The Salt Year" sits in the headline in the same style as the words around it. On a bookshop's page, convention would italicize a book title. Here, only the comma tells the reader where the title starts. Because the headline is bold display type, true italics might be heavy. The title could be set in the bold italic cut, or it could be left alone. This is a convention that costs little here. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **The type is ranked by weight and colour, not by many sizes.** There is a small bold rust date, a large bold dark headline, plain grey body text at about 16 px, and a bold white button label. That is four clear levels, and each has an obvious job. The date stands out by colour, not by an extra size.
- **The two-line headline is set tight.** The gap between its lines is about 39 px on type of roughly 36 px. It also sits close above the body text, so the headline and the description read as one unit.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries)

I worked from the whole image. It is about one screen, so it needed no crops. I couldn't run the crop script because Bash isn't permitted in this session.

**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye lands first on the dark photo placeholder, the heaviest mass on the page. It then drops to the bold headline and the dark button. This reads as a bookshop's event page. It feels quiet, warm and plain. Job (my assumption): get visitors to book a free seat at an author reading.

Color:
- Small palette: yes. It has one warm neutral range (near-black, browns, grays, white) and one accent hue, the rust date.
- Strong color kept to a small share: yes. The only saturated color is the date line at y≈455.
- Clear light and dark range: yes. The dark image, headline and button stand against white, and the structure would survive in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. The warm rust date comes forward, and the cooler gray nav and divider sit back.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The headline and button near-black match.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors: yes. There are none.
- Color not used alone for meaning: yes. The date is also marked by position and content.
- Dark theme: yes. It is a light page, so the line doesn't apply.

No line was answered no or unsure, so I opened no entries.

---

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Restraint with one accent.** The page is all warm neutrals plus a single rust hue, used once, on the date ("Thursday 13 November, 7 pm", around 340–538, 447–463). The one fact a visitor needs to act on is the only colored thing on the page, so it gets found without adding weight or size. Keep the accent to this one job and don't spread it to the nav or body.
- **Warm near-black ties the page together.** The headline, the button (340–502, 625–672) and the dark gradient of the image (340–940, 92–422) share one warm brown-black. The page holds together as one palette and still has a strong light-dark range. The button reads as the darkest solid shape below the image, which makes it the clear end of the reading path.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands first on the big dark box at the top. It holds a generic grey-brown person silhouette, the default "avatar" placeholder, not a photo of the author. Next it drops to the bold headline "An evening with Ines Varga…", then the button. This is an event page for an author reading at a bookshop, and it feels calm but unfinished. Job (assumed): get local readers to book a free seat for the reading.

Pictures (1280×800 image, about one screen, so no crops needed):
1. Every image shows its content, no placeholder: **no**. The 600×330 hero (x 340–940, y 92–422) is a placeholder silhouette, not the author or the book.
2. Full quality: yes
3. Crop intended: yes (the silhouette bleeding off the bottom edge is the stock avatar's design)
4. Figure-ground: yes. The silhouette (about #5C5048) sits faint on the near-black gradient, but that is the placeholder itself, filed under line 1.
5. One rendering style: yes
6. Photos treated consistently: yes (no photos)
7. Icons share one stroke: yes (no icons)
8. One viewpoint and light: yes
9. Texture quiet: yes (only a soft gradient)
10. Honest surfaces: yes
11. Logo clear space: yes ("Margin Books" wordmark, top left, has room)
12. Logo simple: yes (plain type wordmark)

Line 1 has no catalog entry, so I judge it as common sense and there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Pictures: applies (one hero image and a type-only wordmark).

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?** The hero image is a generic placeholder. At x 340–940, y 92–422, it's the largest and highest-contrast thing on the page, so it's where the eye lands first. What it shows is a faceless grey-brown head-and-shoulders silhouette on a near-black gradient, the stock "no avatar" graphic.
   - **What the viewer gets:** the page spends its strongest spot saying "image missing." A reader doesn't learn what Ines Varga looks like or what *The Salt Year* looks like, and the page reads as unfinished. That weakens trust in the event and the booking.
   - **What the viewer may think:** if the placeholder is a deliberate choice rather than a failed load, it's worse. Readers know this as the icon for "no photo," so it looks like a broken page either way.
   - **Fix direction:** put in a real picture of the author, or the book's cover. A photo of the island the book is set in would also tie into the talk. If no picture is available, remove the box and let the date and headline lead, rather than keep a faceless stand-in.
   - **Type and weight:** defect (common sense; the checklist names no source for this line). Major.

**What's working.** The wordmark "Margin Books" (top left, about x 48–175, y 18–40) is plain set type with clear space around it. It reads at any size and in one colour.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the silhouette is a fallback for a photo that didn't load. Check the image URL and its loading in a live browser. Either way the fallback shown here should not be what visitors get.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (every image shows its content, no placeholder)

**Walk (working notes, Interface, single 1280×800 screen, no crops needed)**

- Exactly one primary action, everything else styled lower: yes
- Controls look like what they do: yes. The header nav is plain grey text, but a top-right header bar is the usual place for nav.
- Control edges reach 3:1: yes
- States shown look distinct: yes. Only default states are shown.
- Focus indicator: unsure. Can't tell from a still.
- Focus not hidden by sticky elements: unsure. Can't tell from a still.
- Main content uncovered: yes
- Targets large enough: yes. The button looks about 162×47 px, and the nav links are well spaced.
- Phone thumb zone: yes. This is a desktop layout.
- Shows where the user is: **no**. "Events" in the nav (952–996, 30) looks the same as the other links. There is no breadcrumb and no back-to-events link.
- Visible way out: yes. This is a plain page.
- Inputs: yes, there are none.
- Destructive actions: yes, there are none.
- Everything needed to act is on this screen: yes
- Progressive disclosure: yes
- Fields: yes, there are none.
- Controls next to what they change: yes
- Form layout: yes, there is none.
- Required fields marked: yes, there is none.
- Errors in words: yes, there are none.
- Errors say how to fix: yes, there are none.
- Empty states: yes, there are none.
- Help where needed: yes. The task is simple.
- Shortcuts: yes. None are needed.
- Puts what the user needs next in front of them: yes
- Follows conventions: yes
- Audience's words: yes
- Link purpose: yes
- Sensory instructions: yes, there are none.
- Shows how the parts relate: **no**, minor. Same cause as the "where the user is" line: nothing ties this page to the Events section.
- Consistent across screens: yes. Only one screen is shown.
- Fits the width: yes
- Honest choices: yes

The two `no` lines are one problem. I couldn't run the entries script in step 5 (Bash was denied), so these findings come from the checklist lines and the critic guidance, not the catalog entries.

---

**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a header nav (4 links), a logo, and one button.

**Findings**
1. **Does the screen show where the user is and what is happening, such as the current page or step, progress, or loading?** (also covers "Do the grouping, names, and navigation show how the product's parts relate?"): "Events" in the header nav (about x 952–996, y 30) has the same grey and weight as "New in", "Gift cards" and "Find us". Nothing else connects this page to a list of events: no breadcrumb, no "All events" link above the date at y 455. Someone who arrives from a newsletter or social link can't tell that this is one event among several. Once they decide not to book, the page offers no next step except the nav, and nothing in the nav says which item is "here". Source: Nielsen heuristic 1, visibility of system status. Fix: mark "Events" as the current section (darker colour, weight or an underline, not colour alone) and add a small "← All events" link or breadcrumb above the date. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- There is one clear primary action. "Book a free seat" (340–502, 625–672) is the only filled control. Its near-black fill on white is strong, and it sits right under the description, so the order is: read the event, then act. The nav stays quiet in grey text and doesn't compete with it.
- The button label names the exact action and its cost ("free seat"). That answers the main question about committing before the visitor clicks.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- The focus ring on "Book a free seat" and on the nav links, and whether the header is sticky and hides focused items when the page scrolls.
- What booking does: whether it opens a form or a dialog with a way out, and whether it shows sold-out or closed states. That matters because the date reads "Thursday 13 November" with no year. In 2025, 13 November was a Thursday, so the event may already be over while the button still invites booking. Check the live page shows an ended or full state.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 2 no (shows where the user is; shows how the parts relate), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not hidden by sticky elements)
